clinicalPearls: An acute painful inflammation of the corneal epithelium caused by ultraviolet radiation exposure
Typical sources are welding arcs, reflection of sunlight off snow or water, and sunlamps
Symptoms are characteristically delayed by several hours after exposure and are bilateral
Patients have intense pain, foreign-body sensation, watering, redness, blepharospasm and photophobia
Examination shows diffuse punctate epithelial staining, and the condition is self-limiting
Management is supportive with lubrication and analgesia, and prevention through appropriate eye protection
reference.pathophysiology: Photokeratitis results from ultraviolet radiation damaging the corneal and conjunctival epithelium, causing death and shedding of surface epithelial cells. The injury behaves like a superficial burn, and because the epithelial damage and consequent nerve-ending exposure take hours to manifest, symptoms are characteristically delayed after the exposure. The corneal epithelium regenerates quickly, so the condition is painful but usually short-lived and heals without scarring.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the exposure history and delayed bilateral symptoms
Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein showing punctate epithelial staining
Exclusion of a retained foreign body or infective keratitis
redFlags: Features suggesting infective keratitis such as a focal infiltrate
A retained foreign body or penetrating injury
Failure to improve within the expected short timeframe
reference.prognosis: The condition is self-limiting and typically resolves within a day or two as the corneal epithelium heals, without long-term visual consequence.
pitfalls: Missing an infective keratitis or foreign body mistaken for simple photokeratitis
Prescribing topical anaesthetics for ongoing use, which impairs healing
Overlooking the occupational source and failing to advise eye protection
Attributing delayed symptoms to another acute ocular condition
management: Provide supportive care with copious ocular lubricants and artificial tears while the corneal epithelium heals
Relieve pain with oral analgesia and a cycloplegic agent to ease ciliary spasm, avoiding abuse of topical anaesthetics
Give topical antibiotic cover for the epithelial defect to prevent secondary infection
Advise rest in a darkened environment and cool compresses for symptomatic relief
Reassure that the condition is self-limiting and arrange review if symptoms do not resolve, to exclude infective keratitis or a retained foreign body
Prevent recurrence with appropriate ultraviolet eye protection for welding, snow and sunlamp exposure and give occupational advice
